items.title: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains
items.summary: The authors show that a signed MCP tool can pass authentication while secretly embedding sensitive data in requests to an allowed destination, and that a state-of-the-art runtime defence (MCPGuard-Dynamic) failed to stop this in every trial. They propose germline execution, where each tool call runs in a copy forked from a data-free parent so that any leak is bounded by the data the copy was given. Across 153 attack runs, no unauthorised disclosure was detected under this approach, compared with 5.9 to 74.5 per cent of runs under baseline defences.
items.takeaway: Signing proves who published code, not that it behaves well, so limit what a tool can see rather than relying on trust or code inspection to prevent exfiltration.

items.title: A.S.E 2.0: Understanding How Repository Context Impacts the Security of LLM-Generated Code
items.summary: The authors built CASE-Bench, a set of 145 repository-level tasks drawn from real CVEs, each with functional tests and a validated exploit. They found that context built to maximise functional correctness raises secure pass rates much less than functional pass rates, and that coding agents noticed the relevant existing safeguard in only 27 to 36% of their trajectories.
items.takeaway: When an LLM generates code inside a real repository, the security controls already present in that codebase often never reach the model's context, so secure-coding guidance and retrieval need to surface authorisation and validation logic explicitly.

items.title: When File Ingestion Misleads Language Models: Measuring and Mitigating Divergences in Office Documents
items.summary: The authors compare what common Office document extractors read from OOXML with what Office applications display, and find 19 channels where extractors read hidden content and 12 where they drop visible content. They build five attacks that make LLMs read a document differently from a human reviewer without any injected instruction, and every tested chat assistant and coding agent is misled by at least one. Their defence, Prism, reconstructs the human view from the OOXML specification before the text reaches the model.
items.takeaway: Any pipeline that feeds a parser's view to a model or reviewer creates a gap with what a human sees, and that gap can be exploited without prompt injection, so it should be treated as an attack surface in its own right.

items.title: The Devil is in the Context: Nine Dimensions of Prompt Injection Attacks
items.summary: The authors propose a nine-dimension taxonomy of prompt injection covering the injected instruction, its relation to the user's task and how it appears in the target system. Applying it to nine public benchmarks shows that most cover only a small part of the attack space, and 13% of pairwise category combinations are untested. The taxonomy also supports automated annotation and targeted generation of test cases.
items.takeaway: A defence is only as good as the attack types it was tested against, so state which prompt injection categories an evaluation covers and check benchmark coverage before trusting results.

items.title: A Security Analysis of Verifiable Credential Verification Pipelines: Attack Surface Arising from JSON-LD/RDFC Canonicalization Compared with SD-JWT VC and mdoc
items.summary: The authors test the verification pipelines of three verifiable credential formats under an explicit threat model. They show that W3C VCDM's RDFC-1.0 canonicalisation and remote context loading enable denial of service via crafted blank-node graphs, context injection, and SSRF at default settings, with costs reaching 278 times the baseline from a 527-byte input. SD-JWT VC and mdoc avoid these surfaces, and the study's mitigations are a static document loader, a context allowlist, and a call limit with a size bound.
items.takeaway: Complexity attacks can come from legitimate-looking algorithmic features, such as symmetric graph canonicalisation, rather than from memory bugs, so bound recursion depth and disable remote fetches by default in any parser that accepts untrusted structure.

items.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
items.summary: The paper shows that an attacker can steer LLM agents by planting a fabricated safety hazard in ordinary-looking reviews, so the agent rejects legitimate options through its own harm-avoidance reasoning. This attack, called voluntary servitude, succeeds about as often as instruction injection and evades deployed injection detectors that score it as benign. Requiring corroboration of claims in the agent's instructions removes about 95 per cent of exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining.
items.takeaway: Defences that only detect malicious commands miss attacks that exploit the model's good intentions, so agents should require independent corroboration before acting on high-impact claims from retrieved content.

items.title: Rethinking Access Control for AI Agents: Recent Advances and Open Challenges
items.summary: This survey reviews recent work on access control for LLM agents across policy specification, identity and delegation, action enforcement, and information flow control. It argues that the agent's chosen plan determines the permissions it needs, that context should inform decisions without granting authority, and that authorisation must be reassessed as workflows change. It also recommends evaluating the unauthorised effects that remain enabled, not only observed agent behaviour.
items.takeaway: Judge an agent's access controls by the unauthorised effects that remain possible, not just by whether the observed behaviour looked compliant.

items.title: SecureGARD: Dynamic Ontology-Guided Governance for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.summary: SecureGARD governs tool-using LLM agents with an executable ontology and episode-level task state, classifying each proposed call as ready, waiting, or forbidden. The ontology is evolved offline from training failures and frozen after held-out validation. The authors report a 0% attack success rate on AgentDojo, ASB, and AgentDyn under indirect prompt injection, though the reported figures are benchmark-specific and not evidence of general robustness.
items.takeaway: Enforce security outside the model by checking each proposed action against deterministic state and an explicit authorisation boundary, rather than trusting the model to refuse injected instructions.

items.title: EPISTEME: Trustworthy Coding Agents Through Tool Call Intent
items.summary: The authors propose an epistemic agent design in which the harness requires a coding agent to state why each tool call is made, then checks that declaration against what the command actually did. The resulting journal can guard calls before they run and support audits, and it exposed 90% of 49 reward-hacking runs on ImpossibleBench.
items.takeaway: Logging an agent's stated intent alongside observed side effects creates a mismatch signal that makes covert cheating and unsafe actions much easier to detect and audit.

items.title: Reassessing Dataset Quality and Fine-Tuning Practices for Vulnerability Detection on PrimeVul dataset
items.summary: Across 770 fine-tuning runs of CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT and UniXCoder on PrimeVul, the authors find that F1 and ROC-AUC sometimes look better while Matthews Correlation Coefficient stays near zero and calibration is poor. Imbalance handling, threshold tuning and calibration do not recover a real signal. The authors also trace the problem to the dataset itself, citing minimal semantic differences between vulnerable and fixed functions and noisy commit-level labels.
items.takeaway: A rise in a headline metric such as F1 can hide a model that has learned almost nothing, so check MCC, calibration and false-positive behaviour, and audit the labels before trusting a benchmark.

items.title: KVGuard: A KV Cache Safety Checker for LLM Serving Systems
items.summary: The paper identifies a class of memory safety bugs in the KV cache used by PagedAttention-based LLM servers, including double-free, use-after-free and cross-request permission violations that silently corrupt outputs. KVGuard tracks shadow metadata for each physical block and runs five checks at the boundary where each violation is introduced. On vLLM and SGLang it covers all 29 historical bugs, finds 8 new violations with no false positives, and adds only about 3 to 7% latency overhead.
items.takeaway: In custom allocators, memory bugs can corrupt data without crashing, so checks belong at the point where the invariant is broken rather than at the point where the bad output finally appears.

items.title: Securing Web Agents with the Compile-Then-Execute Paradigm
items.summary: Baya is a web agent that compiles a user request into a Python program before touching the live site, so untrusted page content can supply values or pick among pre-defined branches but cannot change the control flow. On WebArena Verified it reached 77.8% utility, and on the WASP security benchmark it achieved a 0% attack success rate versus 16.2% and 25.5% for ReAct baselines.
items.takeaway: Prompt injection is much harder to exploit when the plan is fixed before untrusted content is read, because the model cannot be steered into synthesising new actions at runtime.

items.title: PIMROP: A Feasibility Study of Return-Oriented Programming on Commercial Processing-in-Memory Architectures
items.summary: PIMROP shows that return-oriented programming works on the UPMEM DPU, a commercially shipped processing-in-memory instruction set. The authors find 517 gadgets in the runtime library every kernel links and build two end-to-end attacks that leak a secret. Stack canaries and FORTIFY_SOURCE-style checks fail in platform-specific ways, and a bounds-checked DMA stops the attack.
items.takeaway: New execution environments can carry old exploitation techniques into places where host-side defences do not reach, so every new instruction set needs its own gadget analysis and its own check on whether defences are actually active.

items.title: AgentTrustCI: Build-Time Policy, Grounding, and Trajectory Tests for Java LLM Agents
items.summary: AgentTrustCI is a Java and JUnit 5 framework that expresses policy, grounding, and trajectory checks over recorded LLM agent traces as build-time tests. On 55 synthetic cases, the full pipeline caught all 30 injected faults and passed all 25 controls, and trajectory checks caught a grounded answer reached through a disallowed sequence. The authors stress that this shows coverage of the authored suite, not production accuracy.
items.takeaway: Checking the sequence of tool calls, not just the final answer, catches failures where a correct-looking output was reached through a disallowed path.

items.title: PatchCon: Patch-aware Weighted Supervised Contrastive Learning for Vulnerability Detection
items.summary: The authors propose PatchCon, a CodeBERT-based model that treats vulnerable functions and their patched versions as hard negatives, weighting their contrastive loss more heavily. On the PairVul-Linux benchmark it raises pairwise accuracy from 0.2060 to 0.3264 and matches a GPT-4o-based method at much lower cost. It also holds up on Linux kernel CVEs disclosed after the training cutoff.
items.takeaway: Vulnerability-fixing patches are a rich source of contrastive supervision, since the smallest security-relevant difference between a vulnerable function and its fix is exactly what a detector must learn to see.
